limitations: No Digital Macaroni hands-on monitor, alert, incident, status-page, self-hosting, or support test was completed.
Independent long-term customer coverage is too thin for a fine-grained reliability claim.
Repository stars and forks show developer attention, not customer satisfaction.

claims.statement: OpenStatus became publicly available on July 31, 2023.
OpenStatus combines checks of websites and services with public status pages, incident updates, subscribers, and several alert channels.
The Hobby plan includes one monitor and one status page with three components at a minimum ten-minute check interval.
Starter costs $30 monthly or $300 yearly, Pro costs $100 monthly or $1,000 yearly, and Scale costs $500 monthly or $5,000 yearly.
Open source code, self-hosting, monitoring and status pages in one product, and developer tooling are the clearest differentiators.
The repository has attracted thousands of stars and hundreds of forks, showing substantial developer attention for the project's size.
The formal customer-review sample is too small to support a broad claim about long-term reliability or support quality.

scoreRationale.onboarding: Creating a green monitor is easy to demonstrate; useful setup requires forced failures, alert checks, customer wording, ownership, and recovery.
scoreRationale.product: Monitoring and status pages fit together well, especially for technical teams that want code-based configuration or self-hosting.
scoreRationale.support: The public satisfaction sample is too thin, and no urgent incident request was tested.
scoreRationale.billing: Starter is clear for a small public service, while advanced identity, white-labeling, and extra pages can make the bill much larger.
scoreRationale.overall: OpenStatus is worth testing for a technical team that wants monitoring and customer communication together. Break a disposable endpoint and keep it only if detection, paging, incident updates, and recovery all work.

conflictsAndUnknowns: Open-source popularity does not prove hosted-service reliability.
Self-hosting gives control but makes the team responsible for operating the monitor that watches its other systems.
Historical infrastructure trouble explains early development but is not a current defect claim.
No monitor, false-alert, incident, subscriber, private-location, self-hosting, export, or support test was completed.
